VENT: The characters in Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs generally have long, cartoonishly exaggerated fingers, as part of the stylized animation. This is especially evident on the main protagonist, Flint Lockwood, and the weather reporter, Sam Sparks. 
This is highlighted in a specific episode of the series, where:
Flint believes all great inventors have big hands and invents a way to give himself a set of giant hands to cure his "inventor's block".
The large, clumsy hands hinder his work, and he eventually reverses the invention.
In the process, Sam Sparks accidentally ends up with the enlarged hands instead.

Questa riproduzione tridimensionale del Laocoonte, esposta in questa galleria virtuale, didattica dell'ITI, rappresenta senz'altro un tentativo azzardato di replicare un capolavoro inarrivabile. Tuttavia, ciò che conta profondamente in questa sede è il concetto e il suo fine didattico. In questo spazio, vale più l'idea: ma l'idea si fa tangibile e manipolabile solo per poter includere un messaggio educativo e formativo.

Questa tangibilità digitale ci permette di esplorare l'opera attraversando secoli di riflessioni. Ci consente di interrogare l'ideale di Winckelmann sulla 'nobile semplicità e quieta grandezza' dell'arte antica, mettendolo in tensione con la celebre intuizione di Lessing: ruotando il modello cogliamo appieno quel 'momento pregnante', dove l'urlo del sacerdote è trattenuto in un sospiro per non spezzare l'armonia formale.

Emancipandoci dalla visione frontale museale, l'interazione 3D fa poi emergere con forza la lettura di Argan: tocchiamo con mano la crisi irreversibile dell'equilibrio classico e le travolgenti diagonali di forza. Lo spazio diviene un elemento ostile, intessuto dalle spire ineluttabili del destino.

Infine, in chiave antropologica e seguendo Panofsky, questa operazione didattica ci permette di indagare la più potente Pathosformel (formula di pathos) dell'antichità: l'archetipo universale della lotta umana contro il Fatum. Permettere agli studenti di interagire con questo simbolo significa rinnovare la memoria culturale. La replica cessa di essere un mero esercizio tecnico per diventare un vero e proprio laboratorio umanistico, dove l'idea si fa materia per formare lo sguardo critico delle nuove generazioni.

-> The only fix I can think of, it to make the objects that are strongly affected by this even more high poly, which will make the effect vanish (as the shadows won't be hitting the polygons anymore creating this grid like shadow effect)

- It's important to know that Sketchfab has exactly 0 light bouncing, which makes environments inherently look fake and bad quality if the lighting plays any bigger role in the overall mood. For the lighting setup I have two spot lights coming in through the window at different angles, one orange and one purple, then one spot light from the chandelier, and lastly a tiny bit of HDRI light to actually light up the rest of the scene, so there are no pitch-black spots (sadly one can't select a single color for the HDRI)
- As mentioned light can't get bright, one can however help this out by enabling tone mapping and increasing the exposure and brightness
- For the bloom it obviously doesn't cast light in Sketchfab. What is also quite aparent is that the bloom will not be visible if the emissive material is a color like: orange, red, pink, purple, blue. Colors that let of lots of bloom are: light blue, greens and yellow

@RottenDesign3D unfortunately this doesn't mean much anymore. AAA studios have become so slopy that its title has lost all meaning to developers. we've had to fire artist with AAA experience at multiple studios for that same reason. And this laziness shows. Star wars zero company a strategy game with isometric perspective should have been super easy to optimise. and yet its biggest downfall upon release was its abysmal performance on even higher end hardware. take studios like Valve, Dice, Face punch... they all prioritize optimised models rather than rely on engine optimisation and their games hold well on a major range of hardware. I've worked at the same studio for a while now and have only been on the receiving end of bad artist coming from those types of AAA studios. from my limited perspective all it shows is that the type of people managing these companies are not the ones you want to work for.

@RottenDesign3D ''shouldn’t have spent that much time on optimization because modern hardware is powerful enough to handle it anyway.'' if someone told me this I'd walk away without a second thought XD single handedly destroying the gaming experience that is. the purpose of engine optimisation is not for developers to become lazy, but to push the experience further where in areas that matter most. I guess I was lucky to end up where I am now, but if I was looking for a stable place I would specifically work towards and seek out studios with good reputation in that area rather than just spray and pray my applications like 90% of seekers in this industry does. freelancing is also a hell hole for so many of reasons I couldn't list them in a day.

@RottenDesign3D this isn't about pushing your LOD's too far or not. they hold zero usefulness in this state. For a stage prop this would still be far too much even though you marked it as a game ready asset (which it is not).
on a flat surface your topology is irrelevant so long as you reduce the amount of thin triangles and don't create concave faces. more than half of the geometry you have here does nothing for your model. 
an acceptable poly count for this would have been: LOD0 =  2.5K, LOD1 =  1K LOD2 = 200 - 500 HLOD = 50 - 100. 

The amount of overdraw this would create surpasses its usefulness
@C.W.R-official- Well. Next time i will simply not make lods.

@C.W.R-official- First of all, yes. The model is trash. It’s almost 2 years old, and back then I was still pretty bad at 3D modeling.

Secondly, saying that it’s useless is simply not true. Modern game development is going downhill. Good topology and a reasonable polycount don’t matter as much anymore. What matters is whether it looks good.

I used to sell this model, and two people bought it and used it in their own projects. I never received any complaints.

Don’t get me wrong. You’re right. The model is shitt. But nowadays, that kind of “shitt” is the industry standard. I’ve worked at 3 fairly large game development studios and interned at 2 more, so I’m speaking from experience, not hearsay. There are lots of games that couldn't care less about some meere 1000 polygons.
Your LOD levels don't have enough variance, the LOD2 could be way more low poly without looking much worse

As an animator and anatomist, i'm not quite comfortable with the amount of hip sway - it seems too exagerated - that's a lot of mass to be swinging back and forth, and the stress on the joints would be considerable. Animals move in the most efficient way possible for their form, and IMHO that would mean a straighter spine with less lateral flexing in the hip region. The animation (viewed from above)  is more like a lizard/croc when it should probably be closer to that of an elephant, as their body structure and mass follow the same laws of physics. Just my considered opinion - the only proof is about 120 million years away...

@studio3dpackage What I do is using Blueprints. You find your car, find a blueprint and than scale it. You really need the left side, top, front and back on the blueprint. Begin with the hood of the car, than do everything in the front the bumper, not the headlights you need to do it later. Otherwise it will mess up your front. Than do the same for the whole car, but leave the windows, headlights, blacklists, exhaust(s), etc. open. If you're done with the body you need to start on the inside. You need to find a blueprint of the inside. Than start with the body of the inside. Begin with were the windshield should be. Like a desk for the car. The go all the way to the back. If you are done with that, start with the details. The steering wheel, radio, seats, shifter, etc. If you are done with the inside, it will be much easier for you. Begin with the windshield. In front. Than on the sides, and than on the back. That is the most easy part for me. If you want an engine you will either make it yourself or buy one. Make someone make it for you. Because building an engine is really not easy. Off course you need blueprints for the engine to. Or if you want to do GTA 5 engines, than just find an image import it as a plane, and set it on the right place. Than Begin on the head and back lights. This part should be easy. But if you want it exactly as the real thing, you need a blueprint. If that is done, the only things you need to do is the plane under the vechile, set the verticels on the right place and than just design, download or buy the wheels. And than you're done. This process takes me about 150 - 500 hours to make. On my own. Remember this isn't easy, it took me 2 years before I could make a good nice and detailed car. Never give up on this. I know it is frustrating but I had that tho. If you never give up, you will make the same models as me. Maybe even better. If you want more blueprints (top-quality), than there is a link in our account description. Just click on my name. And you will see it there. Thank you for your comment.

Oh yes... this table. A marvel of flat-surfaced deception, cloaked in the illusory banality of common furniture. But I see through it. I see the normals.

The vertices scream with clarity—triangular truths hidden beneath their wooden lies. The texture? Pah! Painted pixels on a polygonal prison! Look closer and you’ll see the unwrapped UVs, stretched ever so slightly along the z-axis, like eldritch skin over a skeleton of code.

And the normals... oh, the normals! Reversed in places. Inverted in others. Like the mirror realm trying to escape. I touched the underside once and felt the table whisper back—a collision mesh not quite right, a smoothing group betrayed by haste. To the untrained eye: “a table.” To me: a fractured plane of dimensional betrayal held together with .fbx sorcery.

I’ve tried recalculating the normals. Tried smoothing. But the artifacts remain. Artifacts... perhaps that’s what it is. Not furniture. A relic. From the Old Render.

Don’t trust it. It’s seen too much. And worse—it remembers.
